paper.title: Verified Search with Neural Ranking and Executable Claims
paper.subtitle: Rules decide what is allowed; models rank what remains; claims stay bound to evidence

sections.content:
We study a restrained way to use neural models in checked search systems. A verifier decides which actions are allowed, a small model ranks the allowed actions, and empirical claims are mechanically checked against the same run artifacts used to audit the system. The contribution is not that tiny networks solve hard tasks. It is that checked failures and checked successes become reusable training and proposal structure without giving the model authority over correctness.

The clean anchor is arithmetic sequence filtering. On a next-prime gap prediction task with 30,000 evaluation rows, a learned modular rejection wheel achieves 68.9% top-1 accuracy with zero false rejections, improving on the hand-coded wheel (45.1%) by 23.7 percentage points and on the ungated baseline (9.1%) by 59.6 points. The learned proposer's failure under fixed budget is documented as a negative row, preventing the claim set from becoming a generic "neural proposal wins" story.

The key mechanism is the claim compiler: a tool that reads the paper, cross-references claims against generated trace artifacts, and mechanically assigns each claim a status. Claims lacking evidence are automatically surfaced in the limitations section. The repository trace owns what the paper is allowed to say.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content:
We study a restrained way to use neural models in checked search systems. A verifier decides which actions are allowed, a small model ranks the allowed actions, and empirical claims are generated from the same run artifacts used to audit the system. The contribution is not that tiny networks solve hard tasks. It is that checked failures and checked successes become reusable training and proposal structure without giving the model authority over correctness.

The clean anchor is arithmetic sequence filtering (`prime_gap` in traces). The dataset-first engine accepts new experiments as candidate rows plus verifier labels, generating evidence artifacts before any prose claim is written. A companion memory substrate @paper-holonet2026 is under development for the hypothesis library.

sections.heading: Positioning
sections.content:
A learned component inside a verifier-grounded loop is different from a learned component that owns correctness @alur2024automata. The core loop — enumerate candidates, gate with certified rules, rank survivors, verify the top choice — is linear and auditable at every step.

The gated ranking loop has three comparison frames. Verification-first systems rely on sound checkers but few close the loop on proposal structure. Neuro-symbolic scoring @gao2024program uses LLM ranking without the scoring-gating feedback that turns negative rows into training signal. Code-generation with solvers @polu2020generative uses neural proposal around formal environments. The artifact here is narrower: the model's job is ranking, not generation, and what it learns to rank is shaped by verifiable negative evidence.

The hypothesis library uses vector-symbolic storage @kleyko2022vsa @plate2003holographic @leosc2026 for fixed-dimension rule retrieval.

subsections.heading: The Gated Loop
subsections.content: Every decision follows five steps. (1) Enumerate: given a state, generate the full candidate action set. (2) Gate: apply symbolic rules with machine-checked certificates proving zero false rejections over declared support. (3) Rank: a neural scorer assigns a score to each survivor. Features are tagged by provenance; leakage from verifier into scorer training is forbidden. (4) Verify: the top-ranked candidate goes to a deterministic verifier. (5) Trace: every step is recorded with stable action IDs.

subsections.heading: Feature Envelope and Leakage Policy
subsections.content: Every candidate action is encoded as a feature row. Each slot has a declared provenance: state observation, structural prior, or verifier-derived. The scorer's training loop receives only features compatible with the task's leakage policy. The model cannot peek at verifier outputs during training and claim independence.

subsections.heading: Rule Grammar and Certificates
subsections.content: Symbolic rules are governed by a domain-specific grammar. Each rule has a kind (reject\_action, transform, threshold), typed parameters, and a certificate — the machine-checkable proof that the rule produces zero false rejections over its declared support. Rules are discovered by proposers and accepted only after certificate verification. Accepted rules form a gate set that prunes the candidate space before scoring.

sections.heading: Dataset-First Engine
sections.content:
The dataset-first engine is the boundary between experimental code and paper claims. Before any prose, an experiment must produce a candidate-row dataset with verifier labels, train a scorer against target actions, and log evidence under a fixed schema. The engine runs six adapters against a shared 300-epoch training budget, generating calibration evidence before domain-specific tuning.

This is a quality gate, not a restriction. Any task that can express its candidates and verifier as a row schema enters the pipeline. The engine ensures every promoted domain publishes the same machine-readable contract.

sections.heading: Evidence Matrix
sections.content: The promoted spine carries machine-checked claims verified by the claim compiler against generated trace artifacts. Sandbox domains carry diagnostic claims that track progress toward promotion.

sections.heading: Anchor: Arithmetic Sequence Filtering
sections.content: The cleanest test case is next-prime gap prediction. Candidate actions are even gaps 2--256 plus an overflow action. Candidate filters are modular rejection predicates. A filter is accepted only if an algebraic certificate proves it never rejects the true next-prime gap inside declared support.

sections.heading: Feedback Loops
sections.content:
The main contribution is what happens after the checker has said yes or no. Checked failures are mined into negative evidence sheets, and rule proposers learn from both acceptance and rejection patterns. The rejected-candidate learning loop uses correctly rejected actions to train rule-scoring models that predict certification outcomes. {{C5.summary}}

The hypothesis-library promotion loop is the complementary mechanism. Rules that pass certification enter the rule library and become retrievable context for future tasks, enabling cross-task transfer without explicit rule sharing.

sections.heading: Boundary Evidence
Claim Governance
sections.content: Claims are not prose. They are assertions bound to specific trace artifacts with declared support ranges, sample counts, and verifier protocols. The claim compiler reads the paper, extracts claim references, cross-references them against generated evidence files, and assigns each claim a status.

sections.heading: Ongoing Work
sections.content: The hypothesis library currently stores rules in flat files. A companion memory substrate @paper-holonet2026 under development replaces this with fixed-dimension vector storage, enabling content-addressable retrieval with graceful degradation as the rule set grows. This extension is compatible with the certified-gate framework and not required for the results presented here.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.content:
We presented a verifier-grounded architecture for neural search. The core loop is simple: enumerate candidates, gate with certified rules, rank survivors with a neural scorer, verify the top choice, preserve the trace. The claim compiler closes the loop between empirical work and scientific reporting by mechanically checking every assertion against generated trace artifacts.

The architecture is honest about its limits. Certified gates do not claim to operate outside their declared verifier support. The learned proposer's failure is a documented negative row. The dataset-first engine ensures every promoted domain publishes the same contract. The claim compiler ensures the paper never says more than the evidence supports.

A companion memory substrate @paper-holonet2026 is under development for the hypothesis library, compatible with the framework but not required for the results here.
